About the matter you didn't settle this afternoon...?
Mm.
Only this time, he won.
He was right... I have been using this funeral.
Giada, I don't understand. The arguments before... I can imagine you finding my ideas hard to accept.
But today, about how she should look... what is it you're worried about?
Just because "a funeral ought to be sorrowful"?
You said before that you didn't want to "speculate about Laterano's future" with me. Is the point that you don't want to speculate, or that you don't want to with me?
The truth is you want to change us, change Laterano, don't you? At least Laterano's funeral customs, the way we remember our dead.
...And if I said yes?
One funeral obviously can't do that much, but it's a beginning... At the very least, I intend to begin.
...Giada, you sound like a reformer.
It's only work.
But you want to turn this funeral into... your experiment, or your declaration?
Really, all of this — everything we argue about — should come down to the wishes of the deceased, shouldn't it?
It's because she can no longer say what she wanted that people like us have to... step in and speak for her.
Because my poor aunt died without even one family member to arrange her funeral.
Only me, a useless distant nephew with no blood tie to her at all. And you, one funeral planner at the Ecclesia Requietum Funeral Home.
...That's right. The dead are gone, and no one can presume to speak for what they truly wanted. I can't — so can you?
No one can. Don't pretend you've invested nothing in this funeral. You and I are both using it to pursue what we want—
No... Giada, you're forgetting... no, you've been avoiding it all along — my aunt's will.
However old that will is, it is the most direct expression of her own wishes.
She wanted a party. She wanted someone to enjoy themselves at her funeral. At the very least, on the day she walked into the Notarial Hall and registered it, that was what she wanted.
You don't know the first thing about her. You can't even remember her face. Don't talk as though you watched her make that will yourself. It was twenty years ago...
Is your refusal to accept that the will represents Vivetta's wishes really because it's old, or because it's inconvenient for your "vision"?
You say I don't know my aunt. Fine, I admit it. In all fairness, I was practically a stranger to her.
But what about you, Miss Giada? Before she died, did you ever meet her? Exchange even a single word with her?
That question wasn't an accusation. I genuinely want to know...
—Giada, are you going to turn Vivetta's funeral into your experiment, or your declaration?
He was right. I kept trying to avoid that will, treating it as a joke the deceased made in her youth... not because it was old or absurd, but because it was inconvenient for me.
Miss Giada...
Actually, among her effects, I heard a song—
Never mind. Making more excuses would only be unseemly.
Giulio often can't read people's faces or understand what they feel, but he's genuinely clever, and he wasn't wrong about any of it.
I do want to change this place. Why shouldn't I?
I'm... a Lateran too.
I know, and have known since I was small, that Laterano is the Sankta's holy city. Every Liberi knows it, of course — which is why, however many generations ago, the Liberi came here at all...
...wasn't it to learn how angels live?
It has always been so... and so we shared in the holy city's peace, its prosperity, its happiness. The holy city blessed the Liberi that way.
But what about the future? Who will bless us then?
You've seen Laterano as it is now. Do you like this place?
...No, never mind. Don't tell me.
If you had come here last spring, I don't know whether this city would have looked a little more lovely to you.
But now... it has become this, full of people who don't know what to do with themselves — people like Giulio and me.
Shouldn't I do something... I want to do something...
If I could change this place too, wouldn't that prove that it's my home as well?
As though realizing she had said too much, Giada lowered her head, waved a hand, and turned to leave. She didn't go back into the funeral home; she walked off down the other end of the street.
No one remembered the excuse about "leaving something behind" anymore. The Liberi's steps were light, scattering in the soundless night like ripples from a fallen drop of dew.
Fuuka watched Giada's retreating back, and the thought that "if they'd only talk it out, those two would make up" scattered as silently as the fading footsteps.
She even began to wonder: if they really had come a little earlier, to a Laterano where hearts spoke to one another, would they not have met lonely people here after all?
Perhaps she knew the answer.
The thin light of the waning moon spilled across the white city — a place renowned across this earth for its happiness.
The night mist rose gently, hiding the Liberi from sight.
...Perla! Thank goodness. Have you seen Giada?
It's half past nine already. She should be in the prep room by now.
...I waited in the prep room a long time. She didn't come.
Today's a working day at the funeral home, isn't it? Did she take leave...?

Let me check...
Doesn't look like it. Maybe she's held up — there was trouble on the bus routes in the Stefano District today, wasn't there?
Don't get worked up. The funeral's tomorrow; there's no way Giada wouldn't come. She probably worked late and overslept.
Do you have something urgent to discuss with her?
Not really... I can handle it.
It's just that Giada has never once been late... I...
Oho. Did you two have a fight?
We fight every single day, Perla.
Well, there you go. She thought about coming in and having to argue all over again, and suddenly didn't feel like getting up. "Two more hours!" — don't you think that's possible?
...Perla, are you talking about yourself?

Not wanting to go to work is the most normal thing in the world.
And don't push her too hard. I trained Giada when she interned at the Tribunals — she pushes herself quite enough as it is.
I trust her. She won't drop the ball when it matters.

If she still hasn't turned up this afternoon, come find me and I'll think of something. Until then, why don't you shoulder some of the urgent work for her? She'll be grateful, even if she doesn't say so.
...All right. I will.
...Makoto? What brings you all here?
Your placement is over, and today's a school holiday, isn't it? You could be out enjoying yourselves.
Is Miss Giada here...?
...Hm, did you need her for something? Can I pass on a message?
...Nothing in particular. Yesterday, when we came here looking for something... we ran into Miss Giada working late.
She didn't look... very well. We were a little worried.
Did she... say anything to you?
...She told us about the argument the two of you had yesterday.
...I see. Thank you for telling me.
Was she very angry?
She wasn't... Miss Giada wasn't angry. She just... looked very tired.
...Actually, Giada hasn't come in to the funeral home today. Perla says she may need a bit more rest.
The funeral is tomorrow, and there's plenty still to handle. Even if she can't stand me, Giada wouldn't leave the work untouched. If she doesn't show up, everything gets arranged my way—
One thought of that and she'll descend on this place at triple muzzle velocity! I'll message you when she does, so don't worry.
What about you, Giulio? Are you all right?
Me...? Ha ha, how did this turn into worrying about me... I'm perfectly fine, as you can see — halo shining and all.
Although, if—
If you do see Giada... could you tell her for me that I'm grateful she finished preparing my aunt? And that I'll be waiting here for her.
She's the one who's given the most to this funeral. No one can deny that, and I've never wanted to.
However much we disagree, I still believe her purpose and mine are the same — to present this funeral, whole and complete, to every guest. Even my aunt would be proud of it...
Mm... oh, and although you're not needed today, could I ask you to lend a hand at the funeral tomorrow?
I've requisitioned a few confessionals for on-site service. You know how it is — temporary gun rentals and so on at an occasion like this.
But the confessionals won't arrive until tomorrow. I've prepared the decorations, but I'm worried there won't be time to set them up... It's my job, of course, it's just that right now...
...Miss Giada will definitely turn up.
Mm...
Haah, should I have told her, I wonder... that this is the first job I've had since last autumn? She'd only take it as me fishing for pity... There's no point...
Um... I remember you worked abroad before, Mr. Giulio?
I did. And I made a spectacular mess of it.
The day the Cataclysm happened, I was at a party. When my halo shattered, every child who'd been singing "Happy Birthday" along with me started screaming...
You never want to hear a "chorus" that terrible... Their parliamentarian parents certainly didn't, and my esteemed client wanted it even less.
The good news is, this halo has since put itself back together. Holy Spirit above — I really ought to thank our Law for that, shouldn't I? If only for that, I'll pray He rests in peace.
The bad news is that since then I haven't landed a single job.
Haah, how embarrassing! And children used to love me best!
So you do not wish to tell Miss Giada because you fear she will find you shameful?
No... of course not. Giada is a kind person. She'd find me pitiable.
Would being found pitiable be bad...? If Miss Giada pities you, she will treat you gently.
Ha... You're right, Aigis. But there are times when a person doesn't want to be treated gently.
...There are all sorts of situations.
In our case, Giada might pity me, but she wouldn't give up her position because of it. She'd only refuse me more painfully.
Don't let feelings rule your whole heart; sometimes you must put them in a box and set it aside. People act on all kinds of grounds — reason, duty, morality, even self-interest and self-preservation—
Those are the things my father told me again and again to remember.
I don't know if I ever fully understood what he meant... And now there's no asking him.
But I want to do the right thing, and I want to believe in Giada... What she needs isn't "gentle treatment" either. She must be the same as me...
Once she sees this funeral with her own eyes, perhaps she'll understand me, and understand my aunt, and understand what that will meant...
What we treasure isn't gone the moment it leaves... Don't deny that before you've even tried to hold on to it.
...Miss Giada doesn't seem to be home either. Should we tell Mr. Giulio?
I've already messaged him.
It'd be too much of a coincidence for her to have just set off for the funeral home...
If Miss Giada had gone in to work as usual, wouldn't she have replied to our messages? But we can't reach her at all right now...
Maybe she really is resting...? Or perhaps she wants some time alone...
...I'm still worried. When that powerful monster's presence appeared near the funeral home last night, I don't know whether Miss Giada ran into it...
Even if it appeared right in front of her, she wouldn't be able to see it... If it "touched" her...
It's just too worrying... I wish I knew what was actually going on.
Speaking of which, I wonder how the Doctor's investigation is going...
...Good timing.
The Doctor just contacted me. He wants to meet us at the Confectionery Hall.
On the way to the Confectionery Hall, Makoto noticed that the streets were unexpectedly quiet for a day off.
Going by his impressions so far, it wouldn't have surprised him if demolition parties broke out all over Laterano on a rest day. Yet the streets he walked through could almost be called still.
Thin, unbroken clouds drifted slowly across the high sky, softening the sunlight, and even Laterano's white walls took on a faint gray cast.
Did Laterans prefer to stay home on their days off? So even tireless angels and birds have their hours of quiet thought and rest...
Their destination was just ahead. He let the thin, cloud-like thoughts scatter from his mind.
He hoped the Doctor would bring good news.
Dragging you out on a rare day off — let me make up for it with something sweet. But had you all been somewhere together beforehand?
Something unexpected happened last night, so we went to the funeral home this morning to check on Miss Giada...
Giada... She's the supervisor for your placement at the funeral home, isn't she? But you said "last night"... Did you run into her during your night investigation?
Yes, we did.
Things were rather strange yesterday...
Last night I sensed an immensely powerful monster... We tracked it all the way to where it was, and it turned out to be at the funeral home.
But once we got there, we found no monster. And I couldn't sense that presence anymore either...
It doesn't look like it was destroyed, either... In all these days we haven't even met anyone who can see the monsters, let alone fight them.
And after you reached the funeral home, did anything else happen?
Mm... The only person we saw there was Miss Giada, working late into the night.
And was there anything unusual about her?
Unusual... I wouldn't quite say that. She just... well, she didn't seem to be in a good mood.
Working that late, a poor mood hardly counts as unusual.
When we spoke to her, she told us a bit about arguing with Mr. Giulio over work... and then she left.
This morning we were still worried, so we all went to the funeral home, only to find she hadn't come in to work...
Then we went to her home, at the address Mr. Giulio gave us, and she didn't seem to be there either.
Honestly, I'm very worried... The monster's presence disappeared afterward, but what if Miss Giada was "touched" by it, like that man we met before?
...I understand.
By the way, Doctor, what did you want to see us about today?
I wanted to go over the man who died — the drunk passerby — and exactly what happened when the monster touched him. You are, after all, the only witnesses.
After he "made contact" with the monster, was there truly no reaction at all? Not necessarily a physical injury — any other reaction or change?
Mm... He was terribly drunk at the time and kept singing. Apart from that, I don't think there was anything particular...
...Wait. There was.
We weren't familiar with this place then, so it didn't register — he was a Sankta, and his halo grew dim after he touched the monster.
Thinking back on it now, we've met quite a few Sankta since, and I've never seen anyone's halo go as dark as that.
That's right, that did happen... I remember it too!
Huh... So does a Sankta's halo going dim mean something...?
...I see.
Doctor...?
Ah, let me answer your question first. To begin with, Sankta halos vary widely in form, and some people are simply born with dim ones, so it can't be generalized.
Second, for any one particular Sankta, a halo growing dim...
At the mild end, low spirits alone can dim a halo. At the severe end... Falling.
What does "Falling" mean...?
When a Sankta loses their standing as a Sankta, that is called Falling. But Falling has clearly defined conditions, and what you saw almost certainly wasn't that.
Setting aside the extremes, in the vast majority of cases, changes in the halo relate to a Sankta's mental and emotional state.
As it happens, the second thing I wanted to discuss with you relates to that as well.
I'd like to learn more about how Personas and Shadows relate to the "heart" and to "consciousness" in your world.
After that, I'll tell you what I suspect...
—about where the monsters appearing in Laterano actually come from.
How is it, Fuuka... Can you sense the powerful monster?
Not at the moment... Only ordinary ones. They're a little more active than yesterday.
If the powerful monster doesn't appear, we investigate near the funeral home and Miss Giada's home... That was the plan the Doctor gave us, wasn't it?
If it really is as the Doctor said, this feels like it's getting complicated...
Arooo...
Koromaru is worried as well.
I'm worried too...
Honestly... if that powerful monster's true nature really is what the Doctor described...
Haah. But worrying alone won't help right now... will it.
Woof woof.
Let's deal with the enemy in front of us first. There will be a way.
Giada, you've been here all day. Are you all right...?
I suppose so... With me gone, my colleague will save a great deal of time he'd otherwise waste arguing. He'll get the funeral he wants.
That isn't what I meant, Giada. You should eat something. The bread is drying out.
...Thank you, Rhea.
What on earth has happened to you? I've known you two years and I've never seen you this unhappy.
...Rhea, why do you still wear the Guard's uniform?
Once the insignia are removed, you're allowed to keep it.
But you've been at the Ecclesia Requietum so long now... I've never once seen you in a cleric's habit.
I do guard work here too, so this is more practical... Besides, I might still go back.
To the Guard?
Mm. After I've learned to live "a life without rules."
...Rhea, do you find life in Laterano hard?
Not at all. I think it's good to have rules... But a senior in the Guard told me that a soldier who relies on rules is in danger — in danger from himself.
But isn't it precisely because rules are everywhere that Laterano has kept its peace and its glory? If a soldier's rules put him in danger, then that danger is the soldier's calling.
Life without rules is everywhere on this earth. Are those places better than Laterano?
...After I answered that, my senior only insisted more firmly that I should leave the Guard.
Heh... There's far too much about Laterano that a Liberi can't understand. It would be nice never to have to.

Actually, since coming here... this Ecclesia Requietum has a lot of foreign workers, some of whom can't even enter the holy city. They're always asking me about things inside the walls, especially all the rules.
Their thinking seems much like mine once was — that the commandments and the rules are Laterano's great secret. But facing them, I found I couldn't say those confident things anymore...
Did you work something out?
No... I think I only have more questions. Maybe I still haven't gone far enough...
What about you, Giada? You just said Laterano is hard to understand. What is it you want to understand?
...I don't know. The Laterano we were supposed to be learning from doesn't exist anymore. So what is there left to understand?
Giada, what is the matter with you? You don't normally talk like this.
...I've only discovered that I'm a rather terrible person.
You aren't. Even if you're feeling low, don't say that about yourself... Oh — what about that new funeral you've been preparing? When is it?
Tomorrow.
Tomorrow?! Giada, then you shouldn't be here, you should be going back...
I will go back... in a little while. I'll go.
Giada, stop sinking like this. It isn't like you. When you became a funeral planner, didn't you say you'd change funerals in Laterano? If you give up, who's going to do it for you?
Give up... It isn't giving up, Rhea. It's just — by what right? By what right do I...?
Rhea, I don't think I've ever told you why I come to help at this Ecclesia Requietum so often.
You haven't. If you want to tell me now, I'll listen.
...My grandmother died just as I started middle school. My grandfather poured all his time into the funeral, discussing it with the funeral planner every single day.
On the day itself, everyone gathered around her casket, and behind it stood a very, very tall balloon figure—
Taller than any balloon figure I'd ever seen, with a cartoon of my grandfather's face printed on it.

Dance music played at the funeral, and air streamed ceaselessly out of the top of the balloon figure's head, sending the fringe of hair and the inflatable halo attached to it lurching this way and that.
And it just kept dancing, dancing, dancing...

...I was beside myself with irritation. I asked my father what that was, what we were supposed to be doing. He stared at the balloon figure, his ear feathers drooping, and told me to listen to my grandfather.
I ran away. There was a gap in the cemetery fence, and I slipped out through it.
But once I was out, I didn't know where to go or what to do either. In the end I just leaned against the fence, staring at nothing.
...Does that count as "running away"? With only a fence between you...

Mm. I could even hear the music on the other side of it.
I might have run farther...
But some people passed by. They wore the Guard's uniform, probably heading back into the city.
One of them saw me and came over to ask what I was doing and whether I needed help. Another said I looked awful and pressed an apple into my hands.
...Maybe it was the music beyond the fence, maybe it was the apple. Either way, I told them.
I said I hated this funeral, that I didn't know what I was supposed to do, that I didn't understand what my grandfather was thinking, or my father.
The one who saw me first asked whether I wanted to go back to the funeral. I didn't answer him — he was too strange. I'd only just said I hated it.
Seeing me staring at him, he straightened up, ducked through the gap, and stood on the other side of the fence. And I...
I followed him.
He took me back to the funeral. I don't know what he said to my grandfather, but the dance music stopped. He walked me over to my grandmother's casket and asked whether I'd like to say goodbye.
I shouted at him with everything I had — that there'd be no seeing her again! That Grandmother was dead and knew nothing at all!
He nodded, and said: "Yes. But you miss her very much. You'll come to know that yourself."
He apologized, then took my hand and laid it on the casket. All I remember is that the casket wasn't as cold as I'd expected.
By the time I noticed my grandfather wiping my tears away, he had already gone. Beyond the fence, his companions were gone too.
I never ate that apple. It shriveled up in the end, and I've no idea where it went.
A very, very long time later — after I'd graduated and decided to become a funeral planner—
I happened to pass this Ecclesia Requietum, and saw someone who looked a little like that guardsman.
The next time I came, he wasn't there. The other clerics said the person I saw was probably the curate who'd been standing in temporarily, and that he'd already left.
I don't actually know whether he was that guardsman. I was just a little surprised — so he'd come to work at an Ecclesia Requietum too, and maybe one day our paths would cross...
And if I became Laterano's first Liberi funeral planner and told him about it, perhaps he'd be a little surprised too.
...Do you come so often because you want to see him again?
Not really... maybe a little, at the very beginning. But I'm a few years older now, and I know I didn't become a funeral planner for that one thing.
Not because of some chance encounter, not because of some special person. It was so that... no one at a funeral would ever again want to slip out beyond the fence, ashamed of themselves.
That's what it... was supposed to be.
But I'd forgotten. The only person who slipped out beyond the fence that day was me.
I was only ever doing it for myself.
The powerful monster's presence didn't appear... tonight.
Good work, everyone. Let's rest.
Yes, and tomorrow we're helping at the funeral... We might see Miss Giada then.
Awoo...
You must be tired too, Koromaru. Haah, back home at least we could rest the whole night after investigating in the Dark Hour...
I do not require rest. I can continue investigating while everyone sleeps.
But you can't sense the monsters from a distance the way Fuuka can, can you, Aigis?
I cannot sense their presence, but based on the fact that "areas where monsters appear undergo a change," I can sweep the streets systematically and find the monsters by finding the changed areas.
Wait! You mean you'd go street by street with your own eyes, Aigis?
That's far too much...!
Energy resupply is not an issue. A task this minor is nothing.
Even if you say that, Aigis...
If you don't find the powerful monster, all that effort is wasted; and if you do find it... facing it alone would be far too dangerous.
But everyone is worried about Miss Giada. So am I.
I... want to do something.
Aigis, then everyone will be worrying about you instead.
Exactly... How could we sleep, worrying about whether something might happen to you?
If you insist on going, then I'm coming with you.
My support abilities are necessary for the investigation, aren't they?
Woof...!
Koromaru says so as well...
Do it for Fuuka's sake, Aigis. Good night.
...Understood. Good night... everyone.
...Koromaru?
Awoo...
Mm. I think I know what you're worried about.
I'll remind everyone to wear their combat gear when we set out tomorrow.
Makoto stroked Koromaru, and Koromaru leaned against his knee, warm and solid.
I haven't brushed you since we got here, have I?
...Once the funeral's over, let's go and buy you a brush.
Koromaru gave a short snort, nuzzled Makoto's hand, and lay down beside the single bed.
Makoto sat on the edge of the bed with a hand on his back, and together they watched the waning moon rising outside the window.
Today's the day. Giulio stopped where he stood and drew a deep breath.
Giada hadn't appeared yet, but she would come — in five minutes, in a quarter of an hour, in an hour.
When Vivetta passed serenely through that small white iron door, he would be standing with Giada, because she loved Vivetta just as he did.
What bound them was purer than sorrow and brighter than grief, just as not even death had stopped Vivetta from wishing for joy.
If the dead did not give up, how could the living stand still?
He pushed open the great door before him.
Bright daylight crossed the empty top floor of the funeral home and fell in front of the solitary Sankta.
Hm? Are we at the gun salute already? The guests only just came in...
And why is it coming from over by the cremation furnace... That's not right!
Hey, what's going on here, everyone? Did a confessional misfire? Why are they all knocked sideways?
A misfire... no.
The balloons exploded...
Hold on, those balloons tied to the confessionals were supposed to be moving targets for the prize draw. And they've... all burst?
I just saw all these confessionals holding out their high-five panels, so I slapped one out of habit... I didn't notice they were all strung together with ribbon...

The temporary routes had not finished configuring. The high-five activated them, causing the confessionals to collide, which burst the balloons, snapped the ribbons, and knocked off the silk flowers...
All right, all right, no need to recite it all... Look, there are spare balloons, aren't there? Give me a pump and I'll inflate them while you lot fix the ribbons...
Sir, the kids spent a solid hour getting that done!
I've come to help, haven't I... And I'm your elder, near enough, so show me a little respect! I held you in my arms when you were small!
Sorry, sir, I've only just come home and I'm hazy on my relatives. You are...?
Er... My name is Felice Gaudio...
Do we have a relative with a name that "interesting"...?
Ahem. I'm Vivetta's ex-boyfriend. We split up fifteen years ago.
All right, I know nobody invited me! But fifteen years ago we nearly married. Coming to her funeral isn't asking too much, is it...
Actually, I heard from an old colleague a few days ago that you were back in Laterano, and I wanted to see you. But I figured I'd see you at the funeral anyway, so I didn't seek you out.
...Uncle Felice, do you know me well?
Not really. But I knew you'd be at the funeral.
After all, the day Vivetta brought you by the hand to register that will, I was the one who witnessed it for you both.
What did I just step on... Good heavens, there's a child down here!
...Oh! You're my cousin's boy. Hey, remember me? We said hello earlier.
Why aren't you talking? You can talk, surely? Your halo's thiiiis bright.
What's with pressing your face against me?
...Oh, empathy? Sorry, I'm not in the mood to feel that much today.
Why...?
This is a funeral. I don't like occasions this intense. When a light's too bright, wanting to shut your eyes is perfectly normal.
You seem awfully fond of empathy. So why did you sneak out here too?
Happy, then sad, then wanting to run, and then tired...
...Come to think of it, haven't your parents had a doctor teach you to shut off your empathy?
Never mind, listen to me. If you could shut it off, those two wouldn't be fretting so much. This "abnormal empathy development" of yours — no telling whether you'll grow out of it...
I don't want to shut it off.
You don't? You're this tiny and you already know what you want?
I like everyone.
The young woman shook her head as though she couldn't take it, then took the child's hand and pressed it to her forehead — in her own words, "opened her eyes."
...Why can't I feel you?
...You're worried about me.
Mm, I'm certainly very worried about you now. You really are an idiot. You like everyone? So you cram everyone else's feelings into your head until you don't even know what you're thinking?
Never mind. No use scolding a sick kid... But you can't go on like this. It isn't enough to "like everyone" — they have to like you back for it to mean anything.
How do I make everyone like me?
Ugh, you've asked exactly the wrong person. When Grandpa died they nearly didn't want to tell me...
...If you can make them happy, maybe then they'll like you.
All right. I want to make you happy. How do I do it?
Wow... You really are an idiot.
...Then when I die of old age, throw me an absolutely enormous party at my funeral.
Oh, oh, that's a good will. I've just started seeing an Executor, and I've been wondering what sort of will would be the most fun to leave... That's the one!

Come on, let's go back and find him. I left him over at the funeral; I was going to sneak off alone for cream puffs...
Or here, you have this box of cream puffs — call it payment in advance...
Oh, no, wait, these are the liqueur ones!
That's what happened...?
For... fun?
Ha ha, Vivetta was always like that. Charming, wasn't she?
And afterward? She never changed the will, so she must have liked it too, right? She didn't want everyone grieving at her funeral. That's it, isn't it?
Well, er, maybe...
Uncle Felice... when did you last see my aunt?
A year or two ago, I suppose...
Please don't lie to me, Uncle Felice. I'm begging you.
...All right. In January I went to see her once, but she didn't open the door. That's the truth.
I said a great deal to her, and I know she heard all of it. But she didn't open the door.
She said nothing at all?
...Through the door, she said to me: "Go away, Felice. I can't make out a single word you're saying."
I never thought she would... You see, she was even the sort of person who'd occasionally refuse empathy herself...
...But at the end of that day, she asked me through the door...
"Felice, is this my punishment? Because I was always testing it, because I never treasured it. So this time, once I close my eyes, I'll never be able to open them again...?"
That was when I knew how it would end. She wasn't the only one — there have been far too many cases like it lately...
"Knew how it would end"... What do you mean?
...Giulio, do you... not know?
What am I supposed to know...?
Good heavens... Then I won't be the one to tell you. It was meant to be sealed away... for Vivetta's good name.
Uncle Felice...?
Don't ask, Giulio. I've got your balloons to inflate...
The older Liberi bowed his head, as though the pump in his hands had become the most fascinating object in all of Laterano.
The young Sankta looked blankly around. Those children from a foreign land fidgeted stiffly with the ribbons and silk flowers in their hands, as lost as he was.
They all heard it, Giulio realized.
He looked to the one at their head. The boy named Makoto Yuki did not look away, and Giulio tried to draw a little courage from those ever-calm eyes...
But what he saw in them first was another figure.
Perla found me...
Giada.
How did Vivetta die?
She took her own life. With her own guardian gun.
"Bang—"
The balloon's thin rubber stretched, expanded, swelled until it was nearly transparent, and burst lightly.

lines.st: I remember the time before my father died. After coming back to Laterano, I assumed it would go the way so many things had, and I would forget it.
He was already quite ill before the Cataclysm, and weaker still afterward. I still told him jokes, but I no longer knew whether they made him happy.
Sometimes I even wondered whether everything I had felt before was an illusion. Had this man who always watched me with worry ever, for one day, been happy because of me?
Though he had lost empathy just as I had, he seemed to know what I was thinking, and would speak to me now and then over dinner.
He said a great deal. His soft Lateran accent was like a bubble tangled in waterweed, unable to reach the surface. At least I had a great deal of time to eat with him.
I found a way to take him to the hospital I'd arranged. The doctor hadn't arrived yet, so I walked him a while through that neat, pretty little garden.
That was when the man appeared. Thinking back, perhaps he was a madman, a patient, some lout who wasn't in his right mind.
We met head-on along a narrow path. He wore pajamas and looked quite at his leisure. I smiled at him as I smile at anyone I meet. He looked at me, then at my father.
"Sankta?" he asked, raising a hand and tracing something above his head, watching us with what looked like anticipation.
My father suddenly gripped my hand, so I helped him away quickly. As we passed the man, I heard a snicker. It struck me all at once: what he had traced were Sarkaz horns.
We saw the doctor anyway. There was no good news, and my father said he never wanted to go back there.
Not long after, he died. The last time we chatted, he asked me where someone who has killed their own kin goes after death.
I said I didn't know — we don't know where people who have never killed anyone go after death either.
If killing one's own kin is the switch that parts us after death, then what of killing those who aren't your kin? Killing criminals? Killing beasts of burden? Killing monsters that deceive humans?
My father made me lower my head, and covered my eyes tightly. My eyeballs ached from it. He said,
"Giulio, come with me."

lines.x: ...Giulio? Giulio, are you all right...?
Giada... why didn't you tell me before?
The instant he gripped Giada's hand and asked that question, Giulio understood the answer—
It was precisely because they were at odds that she would not throw that "dishonorable matter" between them and turn it into a weapon.
The question he had put to her was so utterly wrong. Giada was plainly a funeral planner who protected the departed, and who could be relied upon.
Then who was the one loudly claiming the name of family, clutching that forgotten will, and yet had never once truly met the deceased?
On that weary night, the one who spoke the truth was in fact—
...I'm sorry, Giulio, for leaving you here alone yesterday.
As for Vivetta...
Mm, it's all right, Giada. I understand now. You were right.
Is there anything else I can do for you, Giada? I'm sorry for making a mess of this place...
The guests should nearly all be here. I'll leave the rest to you.
Giulio, where are you going?
Me? I'm not going anywhere. The funeral isn't over yet...
Giulio, aren't you going to receive the guests? Perla is helping over there, but your party...
Giada, did Felice tell you? Where the will came from.
Felice? That gentleman just now? I didn't get to speak with him — he was worried about your blood sugar and went to the catering area to fetch you something...
So it was he who told you about Vivetta...?

And about the will...
Giada, you were right. It really was a joke, and I'd simply forgotten. My aunt had probably forgotten too.
...Whatever the reason, there was nothing wrong in you carrying out the terms of the will.
Vivetta died in despair... Is there nothing wrong in treating her funeral like this either?
Amid the light music, Giulio waved at the balloons, ribbons, the donut tower and the sticker-covered salute cannon that filled the hall. And he smiled again.
...We discussed this. No one can speak for the dead, and no one knows what she thought. Perhaps she would have liked this. Perhaps she wouldn't.
Every cleric at an Ecclesia Requietum knows a funeral exists for the living. I simply wanted that living person to be me.
But I'm only a funeral planner, whereas you, after all...
Am Vivetta's family?
You don't mean that, Giada.
Why are you saying these things to me now... Because I look pitiable? Or because you feel you kept something from me and want to make up for it...?
Perhaps both.
You really shouldn't stay here...
Please, Giada. Take the children and go.
Mr. Giulio, we can help...!
You've helped a great deal already...
All right, then do one last thing for me.
Don't look at me...
Giulio... what are you doing?!
I haven't used a gun in a long time, actually... I think I'm frightened. Is that the Law's doing, or am I genuinely afraid...?
Giulio, don't do this.
You don't know what will happen.
I know that nothing will happen.
My fantasy... the dream that everything could still be held on to.
Giada, you were right. I wish I'd understood you sooner — "all of us have already changed."
When that Executor aimed a gun at me and told me to leave the room, when I learned of my aunt's will, when I came back to Laterano — I was glad.
Surely this was proof — proof that nothing had yet gone past saving, and that right beside me there was someone else desperately trying to hold on to all of it... to hold on to our lives.
Far from here, every time I thought of Laterano, my home, the white city, the one miracle on this earth, my heart filled with sweetness and joy and pride.
And now all the joy and all the pride have turned into pain into shame into... confusion?
What is any of this how long have all of us been deceiving ourselves why did I open my eyes inside a fraud this enormous?
Were the hearts I touched real was my own heart real I used to think that since the day I was born I had managed exactly one thing which was to be honest with myself.
As every good person taught me — with honesty, with kindness, with a love of joy, to see and to do and to remember every single thing within reach.
And even so, a blameless life never existed at all.
The one running the con is the last to wake from it. Our lives are over, forever.
There it is...! This is the monster...
What the Doctor said... was true...

lines.st: "My conjecture is that the monsters you have seen..."
"...are manifestations of the mind, born out of the hearts of Laterans."
"The cause of death of 'those who are touched' is the monster's very nature."
"It is nothing more than a wish, congealed."
"A wish to die, congealed."

lines.x: Was it really... drawn here by him?
And it's still broad daylight...
The "full moon" descended upon the funeral home's topmost floor, and the scene around it warped, closing in about the huge, stooping monster.
The monster gathered the Sankta into its arms and pressed him inside itself, in a posture that could only be called tender.
Koromaru raced to Makoto's side and barked without pause at the golden "full moon."
So it really wasn't the moon...
The moon...? What— what is going on?!
What?! Miss Giada, you can see that?

What do you mean...? Why has everything suddenly changed...
Is that... the moon? No, that's not right... What on earth is it... Why does it look like...
the halo on a statue of a saint?
And the thing holding Giulio... what is that?
Along with Giada's questions came the cries of the guests on the far side of the hall, some frightened, some astonished.
...Laterans can see it now as well?
If the Doctor's reasoning holds, it's a product of Laterans' minds... In that case it's hardly surprising that it can affect them.
What do you mean...? What are you all talking about... What is that thing?!
Never mind what it is. Miss Giada, please go and check on the guests.
Don't let anyone come near here.
And what about you?
We're going to destroy it.
We have to save Giulio...
There will not be a second death at this funeral.
Everyone, let's go!
Cough, cough cough... ngh... hhh...
Even so... cough cough... I don't like... suffocating as a way to die... cough cough...
Makoto saw it clearly: the monster hadn't fully dispersed. After flinging Giulio aside, it melted into the shadows.
The huge, warped halo like a full moon still hung in the air, and Giulio knelt on the ground, coughing painfully, groping for something...
Aigis strode forward and kicked the gun away from Giulio's hand.
Giulio, don't do this.
Is there any point... in stopping me... cough... You can't... keep saving me forever...
You won't want to do this forever.
...Why... would you think that? Could Laterano... really go back to how it was?
I really should have... gone with my father... but I... lost my nerve...
I truly... didn't know what he... cough... was feeling back then...
I was afraid...
And from now on... forever... it will be like this... Everyone here... will be like this...
Why... won't you let me... end it...?
The ending... won't change anyway...
...If that's how it is, shouldn't I have died long ago? And not just me — every Liberi, everyone who isn't a Sankta.
I'd really like to say that to you—
...But there's already enough suffering here.
Giada kicked off her shoes and sat down on the floor, beside the kneeling Giulio.
Do you want to lean on me?
...Giada, cough cough... are you going to save me too?
I can't save anyone. I'm not that remarkable.
Giada's voice was cold, yet her hand patted the Sankta's back lightly, helping him steady his breathing.
When the children pulled you out of that monster's grip just now, even watching from a distance frightened me. I didn't sit down for your sake — my legs gave out.
But the funeral isn't over. After you've rested a while, you're coming back to it with me. All those things you arranged — you're responsible for them.
Even if the guests have to be seen off first, there'll still be work left for us afterward.
...Are you hurrying a man who just tried to kill himself back to work?
Stop laughing. In fact, you should laugh less in general.
You don't want to see me laugh, yet you'll save me and bring me back to the funeral you prepared so carefully? After I made a shambles of it...
I think you're absurd too. But right now, I think I understand what you meant a little.
I used to think you were simply clinging to "tradition," self-satisfied and blind to reality...
...Wasn't I?
If you were truly blind to reality, how could you be in pain?
You only wanted to change it — which makes us the same.
Do you know what a rite is, to me?
A rite is language. It's a kind of conveyance — "translating" what's hard to put into words into something that can be seen, touched, felt, enacted.
And anything conveyed leaves something wanting. Sankta rites were once perfect, because you never needed the "translation." The rite was only a dance performed after hearts had already met.
That's why I hated the funeral you designed. Dancing the old dance by rote means nothing — it's only pitiful and absurd.
If a rite is conveyance, then its first virtue is honesty.
And now... you don't think I was lying?
Because you weren't. You sincerely... wanted to convey joy at the funeral.
Not out of stubbornly ignoring sorrow and regret — only because you missed the past so much... and wanted to keep hold of that feeling.
I don't know... For Sankta, was Laterano once a feeling that wrapped around you every moment of every day...?
I don't know either... or I've forgotten. Maybe I did experience it once, but I seem to have been very ill-suited to living that way... My father took me away.
...Did you only want to stay in the Laterano of the past, the one in your imagination?
...Now that you put it that way, I suppose I did...
Ahh... This is so hard, Giada.
Look — I thought designing rites was the one thing I was good at, and see how badly I did it.
You say a rite is conveyance, but I designed all those segments and features and conveyed nothing to you. In the end it took putting a gun to my own head before you'd believe me.
Anything conveyed leaves something wanting. I just told you that.
All we can ever do is try to speak, feel our way toward what others and we ourselves think, converse tentatively, and make uncertain judgments. People who aren't Sankta have always lived this way.
Even with hearts this dull and this fragile, people are... not incapable of feeling others, or of understanding them.
Understanding simply has a price. The effort of trying, the risk of being wrong, the regret of failing, staking your pride...
Losing it all is a frightening thing, certainly. Sometimes I want to be stingy about it too...
...That much I had noticed.
You're hardly the one to talk — you idiot who found out something wasn't free anymore and got so scared you wanted to run!
All right, did you have to put it that harshly...
Maybe I'll fail again. I did badly before, and I might do worse later. Maybe I'll fail forever, and still be failing at the very end.
Don't be so certain, Giulio. That's no reason to give up.
You're stubborn, Makoto.
You're not like me — you genuinely believe you'll manage it, don't you?
Not really. I just don't want to give up.
...You're a worrying child.
Yuki doesn't need you worrying about him. He's far more dependable than you are.
You've rested enough, haven't you? Time to come back to the funeral with me. There really is a great deal left to do.
Life doesn't end... That's its virtue, or its flaw, and you have no choice but to accept it.
...Ah, the warped scenery — it's gone!
So did we destroy that monster?
Mm... If everything is as the Doctor supposed, its essence shouldn't be destructible at all...
But we certainly defeated that monster. Of that much I am certain.
Right, even that eerie scenery disappeared...
Fuuka, what's wrong?!
That static...
The static that's been interfering with my senses all this time — it's weakening!
I think I can sense everyone a little now...
If it weakens a little more, maybe... I'll be able to sense where the door is!
...Such were the circumstances of the incident at the Ecclesia Requietum Funeral Home.

In addition, the investigation found that every witness to the incident has experienced memory loss to varying degrees. Some witnesses' recollections had already begun to blur a day or two after completing their statements.
At present the effect on the central parties involved remains mild. Further developments require observation, and the Fifth Tribunal will follow up.
Regarding the "monsters" reported by the foreign visitors, sightings by Lateran citizens are still limited to the day of the funeral home incident.
As for the foreign visitors, there have reportedly been no new sightings since the funeral home incident.
At the Sixth Tribunal's request, recent citizen suicide statistics are attached. The figure is slightly down month on month, but remains far above pre-Cataclysm levels.
Whether this constitutes ordinary fluctuation cannot be determined at present. The Sixth Tribunal will continue to observe.
And the Sankta who attempted suicide with his guardian gun — what were his examination results?
The paper copy is here. The relevant indicators are normal. No signs of Falling.
...Falling through an attempted suicide is, admittedly, a matter of principle with very few actual cases. The most recent record is eighty-three years old.

"One who takes their own life by gun Falls" is a widely accepted tenet, and someone who takes their own life does, in the standard sense, "erase hostility toward a Sankta" — perhaps more firmly than some killers do.
But in practice, Falling by way of a failed suicide is all but impossible.
Only under exceedingly rare and stringent conditions could a case of "Falling through attempted suicide" occur...
I'm still giving my report? Please don't suddenly launch into a monologue.
Patrizion, I'm discussing work with you, aren't I?
All right... Not Falling can hardly be called a bad thing. A Falling in Laterano at a time like this would be a great deal of trouble.
Haah... And without a Falling there is no trouble?
By the Law's reasoning, the young man we're discussing today met every condition for "Falling through attempted suicide."
...Surely this isn't connected to the aftermath of the Cataclysm as well?
...Best not to draw conclusions just yet. As for the records on "Falling by suicide," raise the classification and seal them for now.
Understood. Lastly, the disposition of the foreign visitors: the Seventh Tribunal recommends detaining them in Laterano for continued monitoring.
On that point... my advisor has submitted a separate report. Keep that disposition on paper for now; I'll speak with the Seventh Tribunal afterward.
Your advisor took part in this investigation too? How did they come to notice this area?
Heh. Where that person's attention turns is always hard to guess...
Though this time it was largely coincidence. Nothing more.
Those students of yours — are they "going back"?
Yes. It took some time to wait for the "static" to fall within a tolerable range, but a day ago they finally confirmed the door's location.
Whether it's connected to that large monster being broken apart I couldn't say, but the door's position seems to have become fairly stable. It hasn't moved in a full day.
I'll see them off.
It may sound cold to say so... but I'm glad to have your assurance, Doctor. Thank you for your help to Laterano.
A small duty I owe.
Besides, I would have sent those children home even if you hadn't asked.
Young people must walk their own roads. Whatever name you give it, binding children's futures is seldom good for anyone.
Heh, are you taking a swing at this old man too?
I wasn't referring to you, of course, Geo.
A joke. Pay it no mind. I should be getting back to the school.
All right, all right — as a parting gift, let me treat you all properly one last time!
May I order anything at all?
Anything you like!
Very well. I recall orders can be placed from a terminal. In that case, in alphabetical order...
Aigis, last time we came along to Makoto's placement you ordered a mountain of desserts. Are you doing it again...?
Lateran sweets really are intriguing. Since we are rarely here, I wish to record as many as possible.
I understand how you feel, Aigis... but Mr. Giulio's wallet...
It's fine, it's fine, order away. If you can't finish it, I'll help!
Giulio, playing the generous host here — have you forgotten you're already bankrupt?
Now that I'm back in Laterano, there's no such thing as bankruptcy...
Come to think of it, shouldn't I treat that Executor who hauled me back to Laterano as well? He does count as the man who saved my life, doesn't he?
Please — isn't everyone at this table the one who saved your life?
Woof!
Yes, Koromaru included.
Hehe... It seems the two of you are all right now. I'm so glad.
This is all your doing, Giulio. Now even I have children worrying about me.
All right, all right, I'm the useless one...
No wallowing.
Giada, don't you find it just a little odd to be playing my guardian, given that I'm actually older than you...?
I am not playing your guardian. Don't flatter yourself.
And what does being older matter? Haven't the two of us embarrassed ourselves quite enough in front of these children? Stop saying things that will only make you blush.
Makoto, don't you think Giada is getting colder toward me...
I don't think so. She seems very kind.
...What are you saying, child.
Still, Yuki... do you really mean to leave Laterano now? You won't consider staying a while longer...?
There's something important we have to do back home...
Haah... For your age, you children carry rather too much sense of responsibility. What is it that only you can see through...
I can understand it, though. Wherever you go, home is irreplaceable...
...There's no need to make the mood so heavy! Getting to know you all in Laterano is already a precious thing... Let's part with smiles.
Speaking of which, Giada, Giulio — do you have plans after this?
...Going to work.
...Being an adult really is miserable...

The funeral home has opened officially, so things should be busy...
There's still a lot to explore in the work, and I'd like to do things differently than before.
Oh, the report I applied to view from the Notarial Hall came through... though what you wanted to know, you already know.
Mm...
After we leave... will the monsters appear again?
Surely not!
Though the real problem was never the monsters anyway, according to your teacher.
...Hm? Why has everyone gone quiet? Did I say something awkward?
Er... let me check my digital handbook... for what your expressions mean...
You actually bought that emotion-recognition correspondence course?!
Yes. Good. I am now feeling awkward.
...If you're bad at something you should learn it! It was advertised at the Notarial Hall, after all...
Unless Giada would teach me? Wouldn't I have annoyed her into leaving within ten minutes?
You're quite right. I will not be teaching you. Good luck studying on your own.
I think... the monsters probably won't appear again.
Although, going by what the Doctor said, that kind of "wish" doesn't simply disappear...
But maybe... that isn't something to be so afraid of.
Laterano will get better.
Of course it will. If even someone as hopeless as me can make an effort...
then Laterano will certainly save itself.
They've gone to the school?
Yes. They said they'd pack up at the dorm and then go to say goodbye to their teacher and classmates.
Are you really going to formally apply for a post at the funeral home? I'm still not sure the place suits you...
I won't turn every funeral into a party.
...I'm worried that place will put... too much strain on you.
Since when are you this candid...?

Forget I said—
Mm. Yes. I'm worried about you.
Telling you... does no harm.
On the day of the funeral, I went up to the roof very early. I was sure you'd come.
Because I still believe that you and I both loved Vivetta. Though... love takes many forms, and sometimes the shape of it isn't very pretty.
It might be seeking joy, or it might be allowing grief... but it's more than that too.
Love is... an effort that never ceases. Being willing to, and then doing it. Never giving up, never stopping, never yielding to disaster or exhaustion... never bowing to disappointment.
So I'll try not to make you worry.
Perhaps there will be days of disappointment again, but they won't destroy me anymore.
The weather is lovely today...
Yes. The apple blossoms have all opened.
Yuki and the others — are they leaving today?
I thought we'd have lots of chances to spend time together... I'd even thought of inviting them along when I go to train at the monastery over the summer.
I never imagined we'd be parting before spring was even over...
Then tell them how you feel, if it's hard to let them go.
Ah, here they are.
Woof!
Koromaru! You're first here, as always.
Koro's full of energy today.
Ever since we stopped the night investigations, Koromaru's enthusiasm for walks has been growing by the day...
Woof woof!
It appears Koromaru very much enjoys walking all over Laterano.
Koromaru seems delighted whenever he sees something new. And whenever we take him out, everyone we meet loves him.
Actually, I've been wanting to take Koromaru for a walk too. There's a route I'm very fond of.
But I suppose there isn't time now...
If I'd thought of it sooner, I could have asked Yuki and Koromaru.
...Shall we go now? We can wait for you.
It's a bit far, so it's all right. Koromaru must want to get home soon too...
But... have you really not considered staying here a while longer?
There are still places I wanted to show you, shops I wanted to introduce you to, and that range practice we arranged before...
As apple blossoms drifted down on the wind, the Cautus girl spoke quietly of the plans she'd made and the outings she'd imagined with her new friends.
The children from another world didn't know how to answer her.
Amiya... I'm sure all those places would be wonderful. If I had the chance, I'd love to go with you.
But if we don't go back... I'd feel like I was running from my own responsibility.
You're going off to do something very difficult, aren't you.
...Yes.
I have liked this time — staying beside Makoto, spending ordinary days... If such days could continue, I would be... very happy.
...But our mission is not yet complete.
Mm... Once we're back, we'll face a great deal of... danger and difficulty.

...But I made a promise to someone, and there's a charge I still have to carry out.
So we have to return to our own world.
I know you won't change your minds.
It's only that getting to know you has been a rare thing. It's no wonder Amiya is reluctant to see you go. She's been very happy lately.
All right. So have I.
But I know the moment of parting always comes.
Doctor...
I'll wish you well.
A teacher always wants to see a child become the person they've truly resolved to be.
Go and do what you believe in. And don't forget — in a great many hearts, you matter a great deal.
I hope everything... goes well for you.
...Thank you, Doctor. Amiya.
Then... goodbye.
Summoning her Persona, Fuuka confirmed once more where the door stood at that moment.
The door had drifted through the seams of space and time, and they had never found nor foreseen where they would finally find it—
right here, inside the school grounds.
Spring sunlight poured down. The grounds were wide and still on a day off, without the least trace of anything unusual.
When Makoto and his companions walked to where the door should be, all their eyes could see were soft petals drifting down.
He turned in the spring breeze and looked back at the two who were seeing them off.
In that very instant, a thread of blue scale-dust seemed to scatter.
Like a tiny meteor, drawing a flash that vanished as soon as it came.
He drew his gaze back and reached out ahead of him.
Out of a ripple in the air, before the boy's fingertips, the door appeared.
Makoto laid his hand on the cold panel — neither stone nor metal — and felt it begin to warm faintly beneath his palm.
The teacher and the Cautus girl watched the great door glow red under Makoto's touch.
With a soft sound, the door swung slowly open.
The boys from another world waved goodbye to the two of them and walked into the door.
Makoto went last. He sensed, faintly, that once he stepped through, the way back to the world behind him would cease to exist.
He stood still a moment, then walked in.
In the sound of the door closing, he heard one last farewell.

lines.st: Through a passage that was nowhere and at no time, they felt a familiar air again.
The wind off the man-made island carried a faint smell of the sea, and the group walked out of Tartarus.
As though waking from a dream, some hazy memory was growing more and more distant.
A white city, a schoolyard beneath apple blossoms — such images slowly faded.
Makoto blinked. All that remained in his mind was a blurred echo, like someone's voice, though the language too was growing stranger and stranger.
Only the feeling in the words still seemed faintly legible. It must have been saying...
"Take care on your journey."
